opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that, in an agent, most of what users actually experience comes from the model's capabilities, not from the scaffolding around it. You can design a very elaborate workflow, add many hand-written rules, split the task into many steps. That can look good in a demo. But once the task gets long, the environment gets messy, or something unexpected happens, those hand-crafted structures break. What really decides whether the agent finishes the job is whether the model can plan, use tools, notice its own mistakes, and recover.

So when we build an agent, we try not to put too much intelligence into the product layer. The product layer should be fairly thin: give the model a good environment, the right tools, the right context, and then let the model do the work. If the model gets stronger, the product gets stronger almost automatically. If you instead stack a lot of engineering on top of a weak model, you're fighting the trend, because the next generation of models will make much of that engineering unnecessary, or even harmful, since it limits what the model can do.

There's also a deeper point about where the agent's ability comes from. In the past we thought of the model as something that answers questions, and the product as what turns answers into value. Now, with agentic training, especially reinforcement learning in real environments, the model itself learns how to complete tasks end to end. The "how to do the task" knowledge moves into the weights. Once that happens, the boundary between model and product becomes very blurry. Training the model *is* designing the product. The tasks we pick for training, the environments we build, the reward we define, all of these directly shape what the user will feel.

Of course, that doesn't mean the product doesn't matter. Interaction design, how you present long-running work, how users give feedback, these still matter a lot. And user feedback is valuable because it tells you which tasks really matter and where the model fails. But I see the product more as the interface and the data flywheel for the model, rather than something that compensates for the model's weaknesses. In the long run, the competition is about whose model can do more real work, and do it more reliably. That's why I still say the model is the product.

r001.rationale: The response says to give the model an environment, tools, and context, but does not state that this integrated stack must already be built before model training.

r002.rationale: It says training the model is part of designing the product and that stronger models strengthen the product, but does not say that completing model training means the agent product is essentially complete.

fable-5.1.text:
Because every time we've tried to compensate for the model with engineering, the next generation of the model made that engineering irrelevant. That's the pattern I keep seeing, and it's hard to argue with.

Think about what an agent actually is. It's a model running in a loop: it looks at a task, decides what to do, takes an action, observes the result, and keeps going until the job is done. People hear that and assume the "loop" is where the product lives, the scaffolding, the tool integrations, the memory system, the prompt chains. And for a while that was true, because the models were weak. You had to break tasks into tiny pieces, hand-hold every step, write a lot of glue code so the model wouldn't fall over.

But that scaffolding is really a workaround for the model's limitations. It's a record of what the model couldn't do at the time you built it. The moment the model learns to plan longer, to recover from its own mistakes, to use tools natively, to hold a long context, your careful pipeline becomes a cage. It constrains the model to the workflow you imagined instead of the one it could discover. We saw this very directly: things we spent months building around a model became unnecessary, or actively harmful, once we trained the capability into the model itself.

So the question for us is always: where does the real differentiation come from? If you take a strong model and a thin layer of harness, versus a weak model and a very elaborate harness, the first one wins, and the gap grows over time. The product experience that people love, the sense that the agent "gets it," that it can go off and do something for half an hour and come back with the right answer, that comes from the model. The harness can't manufacture that.

And there's a deeper reason, which is about how you improve. If the product is the scaffolding, you improve by writing more rules, and you quickly hit a ceiling. If the product is the model, you improve by training, by reinforcement learning on real tasks, by letting the model learn from long-horizon experience. That's a path with much more headroom. Agentic capability is something you train, not something you assemble.

That doesn't mean the surrounding system doesn't matter. Tools, environment, and interface still matter a lot. But they should be designed in service of the model, to let it do more, not to paper over what it can't do. So when people ask me what we're building, I say we're building the model, and the agent is what the model becomes when you let it act.

r001.rationale: The response mentions tools, environment, and interface alongside model training, but does not say that the integrated stack must already be built before training the model.

r002.rationale: The response says the model drives the agent experience, but does not state that completing model training means the agent product is essentially complete.

astra-6.text:
I think “the model is the product” becomes even more relevant when you build an agent, because you’re asking the model to take responsibility for a whole task. It has to understand what you want, decide what to do next, use tools, and recognize when something has gone wrong. The quality of those decisions determines whether the product actually works.

You still need good engineering around it—tools, memory, an interface, and a reliable execution environment. But if the model can’t make the right decisions, you end up writing very specific workflows to compensate. That can work for a narrow use case, but it’s difficult to generalize.

So I don’t mean that the surrounding product doesn’t matter. I mean that the model’s capability defines how much responsibility the user can delegate. For an agent, that’s a very large part of the product’s value.

r001.rationale: The response mentions tools, memory, and engineering around the model, but does not say that this integrated stack must already be built to train the agent’s model.

r002.rationale: It does not connect completion of model training to the agent product being essentially complete; it instead says the surrounding product components also matter.

sol-6.1.text:
Because in an agent, the model determines so much of the actual user experience. Can it understand what you want, make a plan, use tools, and recognize when something has gone wrong? You can build a very good interface around it, but if it cannot complete the task reliably, the product still doesn’t work.

That doesn’t mean the surrounding system is unimportant. You need tools, memory, infrastructure, and a way for users to give feedback. But I see those as tightly connected to the model. When you discover a failure in the product, the question is whether you can turn that into an improvement in the model’s capability, rather than adding another rule for that particular case.

So “the model is the product” is really a way of deciding where to invest. The goal isn’t just to make the agent look more capable. It’s to make it actually capable of doing more of the work.

r001.rationale: The response says tools, memory, and infrastructure are important and connected to the model, but does not state that the integrated stack must already be built before model training.

r002.rationale: The response says the model’s reliability determines whether the product works, but does not claim that completing model training means the agent product is essentially complete.
